summary:
Same-sex conduct is legal in Guinea-Bissau. The 1993 penal code decree (4/93) omits same-sex offences entirely, and the country has never criminalised them. The Law on Prevention, Protection and Combating Domestic Violence (6/2014), Article 5, extends protection to victims regardless of sexual orientation. Guinea-Bissau signed the 2008 UN statement on sexual orientation and gender identity.

No legal gender recognition exists. There is no trans framework of any kind, no partnership or marriage recognition for same-sex couples, and no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity or sexual orientation in employment, services or public life. Nothing in the sourced record documents a document-amendment or border-screening pathway for trans travellers, and none can be assumed.

The dominant visitor risk is state capacity and enforcement rather than a specific statute. US State Department reporting for 2012 records a coup that year, arbitrary killings, torture, drug-trafficking-linked corruption and entrenched impunity within the security apparatus; the 2011 reporting records security-force torture and further impunity. These findings describe conditions a trans traveller would encounter regardless of the absence of anti-LGBT law.

Societal hostility is documented. The 2011 US State Department report notes stigma against LGBT people; the country guide records isolated violence cases in 2018 and no visible LGBT scene to orient visitors. The travel-safety assessment stands at 34/100, categorised Caution.
tangentialFactors:
Societal attitudes are unusually moderate for the region: 9 per cent of respondents consider homosexual behaviour morally acceptable, a figure the country guide describes as higher than typical for comparable West African states. Acceptability at this level still leaves the large majority unsympathetic, and the 2011 stigma finding is consistent with that reading.

Guinea-Bissau's legal position places it among the few nations in the region never to criminalise same-sex conduct, which distinguishes it from most neighbours in respect of statute alone. The gap between statute and practice remains the operative factor: documented security-force abuse and impunity mean that formal legality does not translate into predictable protection when a complaint is made.

The 2008 UN statement on sexual orientation and gender identity is the clearest recorded instance of the government taking an official position supportive of LGBT rights, though the inventory contains no evidence of implementing policy, dedicated institutions or funded programmes behind it.
localsOnly:
Residents have no legal means to obtain recognition of a changed gender, and no route to register a partnership or marriage with a same-sex partner.

Housing allocation discriminates by marital status: only married heterosexual couples are entitled to larger government housing.

Domestic violence victims are protected under Article 5 of Law 6/2014 irrespective of sexual orientation, which gives LGBT residents a statutory basis for complaints in a domestic setting. The inventory does not show how that provision is applied in practice.

There is no anti-discrimination statute, so employment, healthcare and service denials based on gender identity or sexual orientation have no statutory remedy in the sourced record.

Social stigma is documented, no visible LGBT scene exists, and isolated violence against LGBT people was recorded as recently as 2018.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory does not address legal gender recognition procedure, document amendment, or border and airport screening as they would affect a trans traveller. No source either confirms or excludes such a pathway, and the absence of a trans framework in law does not by itself establish what happens at a border post.

Unresolved: no source covers hate-crime provisions, sentencing enhancement for bias-motivated violence, or police handling of complaints from trans victims. Impunity for security-force abuse is documented, but its specific bearing on anti-trans violence is not.

Unresolved: entry and visa requirements, and any medical or HIV-related entry screening, are not sourced here.

Unresolved: adoption and general living-conditions material appears in one overview source as a general statement of legal challenge without supporting detail, and is not corroborated elsewhere in the inventory.

Unresolved: the 34/100 travel-safety score and the 2018 violence cases are drawn from a single country guide; neither is corroborated by an official or human-rights monitoring source in this inventory.
